transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-13
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Recording id: ff-2026-05-13-alcove-001
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (Head of ML, Alcove), Ethan Park (Infra Lead), Lena Ortiz (Security), Marcus Li (Product)

Summary: quick discovery focused on latency/throughput p95 targets, streaming/real-time constraints, and deployment mode tradeoffs (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Customer provided workload shape and SLOs; SE requested artifacts for benchmarking and proposed pilot.

Topics: p95 target, concurrency, streaming token/sec, batching, KV cache, quantization, private VPC and KMS, SOC2 audit items, timeline for POC

-- Transcript body (automated transcript, medium quality) --
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're Maya and Diego from Redwood, we'll run through a few questions about your latency goals and then Diego will ask a few infra details.
[00:17] Priya Raman: hi thanks, excited to talk. Quick context: we're building a conversational payments assistant embedded in our mobile app. Need very low latency for the user path and high concurrency around business hours.
[00:30] Diego Alvarez: great, can you share your p95 target and concurrency numbers? also are you doing streaming token-by-token responses or full response after the model finishes?
[00:44] Ethan Park: p95 target is 250ms for the chat UI overall (time-to-first-token ideally under 150ms), but we can relax to 400ms for longer context flows. We're seeing peaks of ~700 concurrent active users, expectation to grow to 2k concurrent within 3 months. Streaming is required for UX — token streaming to reduce perceived latency.
[01:10] Marcus Li: to add, average prompt size is about 120 tokens; with system + history total sequence often in 600-900 tokens depending on the session.
[01:25] Diego Alvarez: ok that's helpful. For streaming, Redwood supports chunked streaming; our runtime can push first tokens fairly quickly if KV cache hits and batching is optimized. What's your throughput need in tokens/sec?
[01:40] Priya Raman: ballpark today is 80k tokens/minute at peak — which is around 1333 tokens/sec — but with growth we'd want up to 4k tokens/sec sustained for bursts.
[01:55] Maya Chen: thank you. A few clarifying Qs: are you considering hosted API to start or do you need dedicated/reserved capacity or private VPC from day one for compliance reasons?
[02:08] Lena Ortiz: security is a big factor. We need SOC2 compliance, audit logs, and KMS-integrated encryption. Ideally we want VPC peering for Dedicated or Private deployment but we might pilot on hosted if data retention hooks and encryption at rest are fine.
[02:25] Diego Alvarez: understood. For Dedicated we provide VPC peering options and KMS/HSM integration; Private is our on-prem/VPC control plane. For pilots, a Hosted pilot with strict retention and enterprise settings can be an option while we scope Dedicated.
[02:42] Ethan Park: curious about the p95 numbers you see on similar stacks. If I give you our model (open LLM, 7B in mixed-quant), what p95 might we expect for first-token and p95 full-response on a standard Dedicated profile?
[02:58] Diego Alvarez: couple caveats — p95 depends on sequence length, batching, KV cache hit rate, model quantization, and hardware (A100 vs H100 vs 8-bit CPU offload). For a 7B model on an H100-backed Dedicated node with optimized kernels, first-token p95 for ~600 token context could be in the 80-120ms range if continuous KV caching is effective; full-response p95 depends on response length — e.g., 100 token generations at ~200-300 tokens/sec decode could put full-response p95 around 400-600ms.
[03:32] Priya Raman: hmm our target first-token <150ms is promising. How do you measure p95? Is it end-to-end from client or server-side?
[03:40] Maya Chen: we typically report server-side p50/p95/p99 for generation latency (time from request accepted by runtime to first token and to final token). For customer-facing SLOs you can add network and client rendering overhead. We'll share a benchmark sheet with both server-side and synthetic end-to-end numbers.
[03:56] Marcus Li: what about concurrent batching — won't batching increase p95? We need low tail latency for interactive users, batching for cost saving conflicts with tail SLO.
[04:10] Diego Alvarez: yes, batching is a tradeoff. Our runtime uses adaptive batching with configurable SLO targets — you can set max waiting time and batch sizes per route. We also support prioritized routing for low-latency routes (e.g., small batch thresholds) while other background traffic uses higher batch sizes. For critical chat we recommend micro-batching + KV caching to keep p95 low.
[04:34] Lena Ortiz: can you describe the fallback behavior if Dedicated capacity hits limit? We need graceful degradation.
[04:40] Diego Alvarez: yes, we support policy-based routing: when Dedicated is constrained we can fail-over to hosted pool or to a smaller model variant; options are: queued throttle, degrade to smaller model (with quality slider), or route to a cold-store with longer latency but preserved correctness. We'll include recommended policies in the playbook.
[04:58] Ethan Park: on the topic of throughput, can Redwood show token/sec numbers per node for specific model configs so we can map how many nodes we'd need?
[05:05] Maya Chen: absolutely — Diego will run internal runs and we have published model profiles. We'll share tokens/sec per GPU for the model variant you mentioned and estimate nodes for your concurrency.
[05:18] Diego Alvarez: quick sketch: for a 7B quantized model on an H100, depending on decoding speed and sequence lengths you might see 4k-7k tokens/sec per GPU at optimized kernels; on A100 it's lower maybe 2.5k-4k tokens/sec. For a 2k tokens/sec sustained need you'd need 1 GPU with H100 comfortably, but with concurrency patterns and redundancy you'd likely want 2-3 GPUs for headroom and autoscaling.
[05:45] Priya Raman: can we test with our model and some of our prompt sets?
[05:50] Maya Chen: yes, that's what POC pilots are for. For POC we usually spin up a Dedicated pod or a hosted pilot with a compatible runtime, run your evals (we have an eval harness), and share metrics (p50/p95, tokens/sec, cost estimate).
[06:02] Marcus Li: timeline — we want to decide within 4 weeks. Can Redwood do a pilot within two weeks?
[06:08] Maya Chen: yes we can aim for a two-week pilot but it'll depend on security review for Dedicated/VPC. For hosted pilot it's faster (48-72 hours) if you provide model artifact and test data.
[06:18] Lena Ortiz: about security docs, please send SOC2 report and docs on SSO/SAML SSO integration and audit log retention. Also KMS integration steps.
[06:26] Maya Chen: noted — we'll send Redwood security pack and a SAML guide.
[06:30] [Speaker 1]: (mumbled) the cost part, how do we estimate tokens cost vs infrastructure?
[06:35] Diego Alvarez: there are two parts: hosted API pricing (per-token) and Dedicated (capacity + per-token ops). We provide cost modeling for both — for Dedicated you pay reserved GPU capacity and also some usage tiers; Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization to reduce token costs. We'll send a cost/throughput spreadsheet.
[06:54] Ethan Park: any constraints on streaming performance with our client network (mobile over LTE)?
[06:58] Diego Alvarez: streaming is sensitive to network jitter; we optimize server push and chunk sizes. For mobile we recommend small token-chunks and early-first-token to get perceived latency low; also client-side buffering strategies help.
[07:15] Priya Raman: we have some RLHF outputs and hallucination constraints — quality mustn't degrade if you fallback to smaller model. How do you measure quality regression?
[07:25] Maya Chen: we integrate evals tied to prompt sets; Redwood Optimize has quality monitoring and regression alerts. For POC we run prompt-sensitivity tests and provide per-prompt variance and embedding-based similarity measures.
[07:40] Marcus Li: are there limits on concurrent streaming connections per node?
[07:43] Diego Alvarez: practically it's a function of network sockets and runtime; we design nodes to handle thousands of concurrent streams but throughput per node will be the limiter (tokens/sec). We'll size the infra based on your concurrency and token/sec peaks.
[07:58] [00:08:00] Priya Raman: (pauses) also curious about latency percentile reporting — do you provide p95 across regions? we have users in NA and EU.
[08:07] Maya Chen: yes, telemetry per-region, per-route, and token-level cost/latency breakdowns in Redwood Console. You can set rollouts by region and automatic fallback.
[08:18] Ethan Park: for the POC can we run on both Hosted and Dedicated to compare real numbers?
[08:22] Diego Alvarez: that's a great approach; run same workload on hosted baseline and then on a Dedicated config and compare server p95/throughput/cost.
[08:32] Priya Raman: perfect. Can you capture the exact test plan we'll use? we'll share prompt set and sample users.
[08:38] Diego Alvarez: yes we'll draft a test plan: 1) synthetic token/sec ramp to 4k tokens/sec, 2) workload-shaped concurrent users (simulate 2k active users), 3) streaming end-to-end p95 measurements (first-token + final), and 4) failure/retry scenarios.
[08:54] Lena Ortiz: about logging — do you provide request-level IDs for audit and exports?
[08:59] Maya Chen: yes request IDs, full audit logs (configurable retention), and we can stream logs to your SIEM via secure connectors.
[09:08] Priya Raman: any known gotchas with KV cache for multi-tenant workloads?
[09:12] Diego Alvarez: cache hit effectiveness degrades if prompts are highly unique; we recommend prefix caching for system prompts and session caching for returning users. For multi-tenant we isolate caches per-tenant on Dedicated.
[09:28] Marcus Li: what about quantization—do you do post-training or is it per-deploy dynamic?
[09:33] Diego Alvarez: we support static quantization profiles and dynamic execution paths; the runtime picks the best kernel and quant path for the model. For POC we'll test different quant levels and measure both latency and quality impact.
[09:48] [09:48] Marcus Li: ok sounds good. Anything else from the team?
[09:52] Priya Raman: one more — streaming consistency: sometimes clients get duplicate tokens on reconnect, how do you handle resume?
[09:59] Diego Alvarez: we surface chunk offsets and sequence tokens so clients can resume without duplication, plus idempotency keys for requests. We'll include client integration notes in the POC playbook.
[10:12] Maya Chen: quick recap and next steps: Diego will run initial internal tokens/sec estimate and share model performance sheet; we'll send security pack to Lena; we'll schedule pilot scaffolding and aim for a pilot kickoff in two weeks; SE to prepare test plan and cost estimate.
[10:28] Ethan Park: assign owners?
[10:30] Maya Chen: owners: Redwood SE (Diego) for benchmark runs and test plan, Maya to coordinate pilot and pricing, Lena will lead security review and Priya will provide prompt sets.
[10:42] Marcus Li: thanks all, excited to see results.
[10:45] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with artifacts and a calendar invite.

-- End of transcript --
